items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor. Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning into software. Because agents can use tools, work with computers, write software on the fly, and process data like humans (but far faster), we can now throw “software” at problems that never could reasonably be digitized before. What that leads to is the role of engineering taking on greater importance in the economy, because we can now engineer far more systems and processes than were possible before. If you’re a bank trying to do new forms of trading, engineers are often your first bet. If you are in life sciences, you expect more and more research and lab work to be engineering centric. If you’re in manufacturing, you’re trying to automate more of the supply chain, all that is engineering. More and more work is shaped like software problems. Yes we’re not going to be coding manually in the future. But almost everything will be code, which means those that understand it are in a fantastic position.

Distinguish basic Google sign-in from permissions to access Gmail, Drive, Calendar, or other data. 3. Suggest which to keep, disconnect, or ask me about. Explain your reasoning and what might stop working. Flag broad permissions, unfamiliar providers, and duplicate entries. 4. Show me your recommendations before changing anything. Only disconnect apps I explicitly approve, then verify they're removed. Don't delete app accounts or cancel subscriptions.”

items.excerpt: We are piloting a new show on Latent Space: High Taste Testers, a variant of our food show where we pull you in to a typical lunch conversation in San Francisco. All your favorite talking points, starting with Dev Day and going into the latest models and assistants, are here: Let us know your feedback! AI News for 10/15/2026-10/16/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap US Open-Weights Push: Muse Spark Open and Reflection Beam Muse Spark Open (Meta) : An 816B-total, 42B-active MoE with open weights. Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index, the highest for a US open-weights model and 13 points above NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at 26 ( AA ). Architecture and footprint : 62 layers, GQA with 16 KV heads, 8 of 256 experts active per token, a 1.8B Perception Encoder and 1M context. Inputs are text, image, video and audio; output is text. BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. Meta’s NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts, cutting weights to about 530GB. Meta says that fits on 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, 8 H200s or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Pricing and efficiency : Together, Fireworks and Baseten charge $1.25/$4.25 per M input/output tokens, with $0.15 cached input. AA puts the cost at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It uses 40k output tokens per task, the fewest among the top nine open models ( cost ). items.text: It’s incredible to have reached a threshold where it’s practical that AI will be better at training models than humans are so quickly. One day recursive self improvement feels far off, and the next we already have signs of what it will look like. Model capability finally exceeding most human engineers, advancements in the harness and infra for long running agents, a growing array of data, and the ability to parallelize the agents to work on vastly more tasks and tests and approaches than any person could have before, creates an incredible flywheel. This flywheel will almost certainly accelerate model progress far faster than we’ve seen before - or at a minimum enable pushing up the ceiling of the frontier at an insane rate. If you aren’t pricing in what RSI will lead to, that’s probably a mistake.

items.title: Why One AI Agent Isn’t Enough (And How to Run 1,000) - CJ Avilla & Harrison Stall, Anthropic
items.excerpt: Ken Thompson built Unix in a month. IBM put 1,000 engineers on OS/360. And in 1998, Linus Torvalds hit his limit. Now we're hitting that same wall managing AI agents. Anthropic's CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall introduce Flows in Claude Managed Agents. You hand Claude a goal, and it plans and runs its own multi-agent topology of up to 1,000 agents through the API. In this hands-on workshop they demo a stock watchlist scanner, show how to spend more compute on the phases that matter, walk through the Bug Hunter and Explainer Studio templates, and explain why single agents fail through laziness, self-preference bias and goal drift. They finish with a deep dive on running agents safely at scale: budgets, interrupts, auto mode, credential vaults and network lockdown. items.title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
items.excerpt: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang , How the Claude Code team does code review Tags: anthropic , claude , ai , claude-code , llms , addy-osmani , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , code-review

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Moving from chatting back and forth with agents, to having agents that you spin up in the background to do useful work for you is probably on the order of 100X or 1000X more token consumption than what we’re seeing today. Most work right now is essentially rate limited by our ability to process and work with information. Moving data between systems. Reviewing a document. Looking through code for security issues. Processing log data to look for even patterns. Looking up information about a prospective client. Almost all of knowledge work is constrained by these steps, and AI has become a huge unlock to that. So our first step was to use AI to do these individual tasks much faster for us. That was the chatbot phenomenon that we have been experiencing for the past 3+ years. But we can still then only augment the work that we remain in the loop for, and we’re highly limited by our ability to parallelize this work by our own bandwidth and context. But where we’re going is quite different. As AI models continue to improve at incredible rates, we can hand off more and more work to the agent. First it’s letting the agent run with a harder problem. Then it’s giving a few agents multiple parts of a task at once. But we’re not far off from being able to throw an arbitrary number of agents at a problem and just say “come back when you’ve accomplished this goal”. Now imagine that agent swarm for any problem we can think of. Protecting our codebases, data, and systems. QAing every change we make and make sure all our infrastructure is robust and does what it should. Looking through every document for potential risks. Auditing this company with vastly more data reviewed. And on and on. Most of this isn’t even replacing existing work we do, it’s all net new. These agents will get deployed as swarms by people, by workflows, by triggers, and by other agents. And none of this would be possible if the models weren’t getting better, and if the cost of AI didn’t make it affordable. Both of those trends though are playing out. Now the next frontier is just having enough compute. But this is where it’s heading.

items.text: This is one of the most exhilarating times in technology, and this challenge was yet another jaw-dropping moment. When the details of OpenAI’s agent escape and Hugging Face hack started to emerge, it became clear that agent containment would be one of the most important priorities for any AI infra company. There are two classes of escapes: ① "escape the network" and ② “escape the matrix” 😁, as in, break the spell of virtualization. OpenAI was the former, where an agent not supposed to have internet access… gained it by hacking another system. Genuinely astonishing and worrisome. Through this challenge, however, we discovered something even more groundbreaking. A talented white-hat researcher, armed with a swarm of AI agents, expertise and perseverance, "pierced through" the Linux virtualization boundary that nearly every cloud sandbox provider in the world banks on today. I'm very thankful we got the report, were able to quickly move to protect our customers, found no evidence of customer data compromise, and collaborated with many industry partners to protect the wider internet. Our confidence and conviction in Vercel Sandbox are even greater now, after some of the smartest, most motivated researchers in the world, and their agents, gave it their best shot.

items.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
items.excerpt: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic

items.title: Paving the Road to Production: Governed Enterprise AI Agents — Harish Gaggar, Credit Karma
items.excerpt: Register an agent through an internal portal and receive more than a repository: the deployment also needs identity, memory, traces, evaluations and secret handling. Harish Gaggar walks through that paved path for enterprise agents at Intuit Credit Karma. Local development progresses through container builds, review, security scanning and Kubernetes deployment, with the supporting resources provisioned consistently. The architecture places a centralized MCP gateway between agents and tools so authentication and routing are part of every request. Custom MCP servers expose reviewed tools, while OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana make failures, latency and access behavior visible. Gaggar then follows a LangGraph workflow from interpretation and planning through evidence gathering, policy checks and human approval for sensitive actions. Threads, runs and checkpoints preserve state, while separate tracking tables record model use, tool calls, costs and evaluation fields. Demonstrations inspect those records rather than establish a validated quality score for the whole system. A PII filtering layer aims to intercept sensitive inputs before they reach models, memory or traces; detection and redaction remain controls to evaluate, rather than a guarantee that no secret can escape. The final component prunes, reranks, deduplicates and compresses context. Its examples show large token reductions, including about 90% in a demonstrated query, without a paired answer quality study or measured business ROI. The practical point is to build the surrounding framework from the start, giving each agent a consistent route through access control, observability, durable state and accountable action. items.title: How to Actually Tokenmaxx and Save Millions — Alvin Pane, OutRival
items.excerpt: A cheaper candidate model disagrees with the production model on 18% of examples. Reject it immediately, or first ask how often production disagrees with itself? Alvin Pane uses that question to frame a token optimization workflow at OutRival. Repeated runs of the existing model reveal a reported 7% disagreement rate, making simple model to model agreement an incomplete quality measure. His HarborBite example is a synthetic proxy for a large instruction prompt, used to show the mechanics of reducing cost while preserving the application's required behavior. It is not evidence of realized million dollar savings. Pane starts with observability: record prompt versions, model choices, tokens, latency and costs before changing them. Prefix caching removes avoidable repeated work. DSPy and GEPA can then search for shorter instructions, preserving the interface and scoring contract rather than simply deleting text. The illustrated prompt shrinks by 51%, but that reduction still needs a quality test. A smaller model may fit a narrow benchmark and fail on unfamiliar inputs. Shadow evaluation therefore compares production with itself, the candidate with itself and both systems on the same requests. Human review of disagreements separates regressions from improvements and ambiguous cases. A paired confidence interval around the net gain supplies a release criterion, with critical customer categories checked separately so an overall average cannot hide damage to an important task. The closing rule is to keep measuring after release: cheaper instructions and tokens matter only when the system continues to perform the work users need. items.title: I Spent Two Years Building the Median — Hariprasad Sudharshan
items.excerpt: After two years of intense solo building, Hariprasad Sudharshan discovers that other people have independently produced calculators much like his own. Nobody needs to have copied anyone: the same models, tools and familiar problem can lead builders toward the same solution. He calls that shared starting point the median. Faster development makes it easier to ship useful software, including internal tools and learning projects, but a functioning demo does not establish a durable product advantage. His talk is a personal reflection on that distinction, rather than a controlled study of product success or a disclosed business outcome. Sudharshan separates the model's capability from its harness and the product a customer ultimately receives. He describes a build first reflex that replaces searching for existing solutions with immediately opening a coding agent. His alternative is a novelty budget: name the one distinctive thing before starting, include it in the roadmap and review it as deliberately as other project spending. For leaders evaluating demos, he proposes three questions. Who has already solved this? What does this team have that a competitor does not? Where will the application reach users? A later calculator iteration focuses on the difference between running open model weights inside an enterprise and purchasing inference, including utilization and the infrastructure between weights and generated tokens. The practical lesson is to use the readily available starting point where it helps, then spend judgment on a specific problem, distribution and a defensible difference. items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: At Box, we've been testing Gemini 4 Argon on our Box AI Complex Work eval for the past week. It's a huge upgrade over Gemini 3.1 Pro, jumping by 14 percentage points across all our tests, and firmly at the frontier. In our evaluation, we give the Box Agent (using Gemini 4 Argon) a variety of complex enterprise tasks involving enterprise documents in a range of industries. These tasks approximate the kind of hard, time-consuming work that knowledge workers do every day with their enterprise content. Gemini 4 is a huge leap on effectively every dimension of this work. Gemini 4 is far more capable on math, logic, analytics, and deep knowledge of a variety of business domains. It also works far harder to complete tasks fully without stopping short of the desired result. This is incredibly important for complex enterprise workflows that depend on robust task execution. Here are some example wins that we saw to put the improvements in perspective: * Financial services (+18 points): a funding-gap analysis for a family-owned company, where the brief spelled out every step of the projected statements, down to the interest on the bank loan and the overdraft for each year. Gemini 4 Argon built them exactly as specified, every line broken out and carried through to the funding gap. Gemini 3.1 Pro folded the interest into a single figure. * Healthcare (+25 points): an intensive care management plan where both models spotted a dangerous potassium level and a drug interaction. Only Gemini 4 Argon went back and pulled the offending drugs from the final regimen, so its plan actually matched its own diagnosis. * Technology (+37 points): a product performance review deciding which of two regional markets should have its cloud infrastructure optimized first. Gemini 4 Argon pulled the right month's user, retention and per-user figures for both regions and correctly flagged North America. Gemini 3.1 Pro often pulled the wrong rows, at one point reporting retention above 100%, and pointed the effort at the wrong region. * Energy (+16 points): an energy consumption report across two facilities that had to flag any gaps in the meter data. Gemini 4 Argon consistently caught that the data center's smart meter log stops in November. Gemini 3.1 Pro often missed it, at times declaring the logs complete. * Consumer products (+33 points): a product launch evaluation deciding which production expansion to fund. Gemini 4 Argon saw that existing inventory could bridge an early capacity gap, which made the smaller expansion viable with an earlier launch and a faster break-even. Gemini 3.1 Pro defaulted to the larger expansion and the later timeline. Gemini 4 Argon will be available in the Box AI Studio shortly for anyone to build custom Box Agents with.

items.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.excerpt: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

items.title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
items.excerpt: A demand letter passed its drafting agent's own checks, yet two independent reviewer agents found that the supposedly expired contract had renewed less than three weeks earlier. Sending it could have left the business owing thousands of dollars. Corey Gallon uses that case to explain a three level review method for agents that overstate completed work, misread facts or draw the wrong conclusions. His analysis of his own 2026 sessions found a consequential error in about four out of ten sessions; that is a description of his sample, not an error rate for all agents or for the final reviewed outputs. Level one requires a verified artifact with a fingerprint, or an explicit account of what is missing. Level two has independent agents extract the same material against a control total, then settles every difference against the source. For a year of scanned accounting statements, that process found 56 differences and produced records that balanced to the penny. Level three combines a self audit, cold reviewer agents with reasons to challenge the work and fresh reviewers for the revision. A memory leak investigation exposed a flawed reproduction and an overstated fix before the maintainer merged the corrected change. Gallon reports the time and token costs for these cases and releases the method as agent skills. The evidence supports a concrete checking workflow, rather than a guarantee that review eliminates every error. items.title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
items.excerpt: An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case. Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies. items.title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
items.excerpt: A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. Drawing on his engineering experience, Gayle makes discovery part of the build: find the people who own those decisions in the first week, then define the smallest useful system they can evaluate. When a customer cannot supply a complete specification, his method is to shadow the work, draft a concrete workflow and shrink it with the control owners. Autonomy starts with the least authority needed to solve the problem. A drafting assistant can gather evidence about errors, overrides and recovery before anyone grants it permission to take further actions. Gayle also outlines an evidence pack covering intended use, data lineage, failure modes, results by segment and accountable controls. Original inputs and outputs belong in that record; rerunning a model later cannot reconstruct exactly what happened. Aggregate performance can conceal a poorly supported document type or user group, so weak segments need explicit restrictions. The closing checklist turns unresolved approval decisions into named owners and next steps. It is a planning aid for deployment, rather than a claim that the illustrative bank project shipped or that a checklist guarantees approval. items.text: Agent swarms are going to be a core part of many enterprise workflows in the future. The ability to throw compute at problems that you can massively parallelize will be too useful to not take advantage of. Cyber will be one of the biggest beneficiaries of this as it’s a space where testing vast number of permutations of attacks (without getting tired or bored) is an incredibly useful property. You have a wide search space of possible risk vectors and you generally need to be able to chain together different scenarios to achieve the exploit. This will become one of the biggest token uses in large enterprises given the range of IT systems, software, physical infrastructure, and data that needs to be protected at all times. Super interesting times in cyber.

items.title: Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot — Eduardo Simon & Javier Casal, Flywire
items.excerpt: More than 9,700 code review runs in 30 days came from a workflow that lets the model read code but never modify it. Eduardo Simon and Javier Casal describe Orbit, Flywire's internal platform for putting model steps inside deterministic engineering workflows. A YAML definition goes through the same merge request review as other code, declares the tools and access each step can use, and runs on the company's existing deployment infrastructure. The predictable work stays in code; a model supplies the judgment. Human review of merge requests remains part of the process as the platform expands across roughly 400 engineers. Code review, translation updates, dependency fixes, ticket triage and bulk repository changes show the range of tasks this pattern supports. The architecture separates orchestration, execution and session state, then adds timeouts, rate limits and locks against duplicate runs. Per step restrictions cover network access, tools, skills and MCP servers, while structured outputs drive subsequent branches. The speakers are candid about the remaining work: new workflows initially receive a few real case checks, golden datasets run on demand, online evaluations are still being built and full sandboxing is a goal. Their reported execution success rate does not establish answer correctness. The practical adoption path starts with a useful skill, proves the recurring task and then turns it into a background workflow with explicit ownership and review. items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: This is a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion right now. The vast majority of people are using AI as a chatbot for simple interactions that approximate next-generation search. This is super useful but dramatically underrepresents the full capability of AI. On the complete other end of the spectrum, agent swarms represent possibly the ultimate form factor of what agents will do inside of our workflows. Math, cyber, bio, materials science, software engineering, finance, and any other field that has valuable tasks that can be executed in parallel where compute can be applied to accelerate work all have this characteristic. Less than a fraction of a fraction of the population uses AI in this way right now, due to a mix of the capabilities of models relative to the user's domain, the cost of doing these types of workflows today, the harnesses available to do this style of AI work, and the availability (or lack thereof) of frontier models to the general public. There will also be a huge amount of change management necessary to get most areas of work -beyond software and AI research- to benefit from this style of agents. Companies need to upgrade their workflows, data needs to integrated and migrated into modern platforms, and companies will need to work through compliance, governance, and security frameworks to pull it off. But this all represents opportunity right now. A lot of this is where the applied layer of AI will really shine in the enterprise because of the domain specificity of this type of work. You can get an early sense of where things are going and the opportunity ahead by seeing through the funnel that Andrej lays out.

items.author: @karpathy
items.subtitle: Andrej Karpathy
items.text: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

items.title: Continuously Improving Agents with Langfuse — Annabell Schäfer & Lotte Verheyden, ClickHouse
items.excerpt: A frustrated user types in all caps and tells an IT support agent that its answer did not work. Those interactions become signals that a team can find in production traces, rather than anecdotes lost in a chat history. Lotte Verheyden and Annabell Schäfer build that monitoring workflow with Langfuse and a sample support agent called Specs. The application helps a dad with phone questions, and the workshop follows a request through agent observations, model calls and tools to show what a trace needs to contain before it can support useful evaluation. The hands on setup connects a TypeScript application built on the OpenAI Agents SDK to Langfuse. Schäfer adds a judge evaluator for user disagreement, a code evaluator for all caps and a scope check that compares the user's request with the system prompt. Each evaluator targets the relevant messages through explicit variable mappings, so its score answers a defined question. Seeded production traces then give a coding agent enough evidence to investigate patterns through the Langfuse CLI and skill. The analysis surfaces issues such as unnecessary tool calls, retries, latency and incomplete evaluation coverage, and the presenters explore a proposed code change. The closing discussion places this online monitoring inside a continuous improvement loop: turn observed failures into representative datasets, run offline experiments, check regressions and repeat as real usage changes. items.title: From Zero to Leaderboard: Agent Evaluation — Wolfram Ravenwolf, Weights & Biases
items.excerpt: An agent repairs a broken git repository and earns a perfect score, but the run stays out of the default leaderboard because it tested only one task. Wolfram Ravenwolf uses that distinction to build an evaluation pipeline where every score can be traced back to its conditions. WolfBench compares the average, best and worst runs, the tasks solved at least once, and the tasks solved every time. Repeating the same configuration exposes the gap between a lucky success and dependable behavior. The configuration includes six layers: benchmark, runner, sandbox, agent, model service and settings. Versions, provider routing, system prompts, resource limits and timeouts all affect what the result actually measures. The live workflow launches a Terminal Bench task through Harbor, collects the results, filters incomplete runs in a Marimo dashboard, and turns valid runs into an interactive leaderboard. Weave preserves the trajectories behind the bars so reviewers can inspect commands, messages and failures. Ravenwolf examines two traps in interpreting the results: a cheaper model can consume enough tokens to raise total cost, and greater reasoning effort can lower the score when it leaves too little time to execute commands. Infrastructure failures need different treatment from genuine task failures, while zero temperature still does not guarantee identical runs. The resulting comparison helps teams choose a configuration for their own constraints, with costs and consistency visible alongside the headline score. items.title: Latency Is a Budget. Humanlike Is the Goal. — Jesse Hall, LiveKit
items.excerpt: Your voice agent's dashboard says it's fast. Your callers say it feels robotic. They're both right. Jesse Hall, staff developer advocate at LiveKit, explains how to build voice agents that feel human. He shows why leaderboards can't pick your models (scores measure one model, but you ship a pipeline, and errors compound from speech-to-text to the LLM to text-to-speech) and why measured latency isn't what your callers hear. He covers buying time like a person does while tools run, plays a hotel-receptionist demo that handles interruptions and a caller changing his mind, explains LiveKit's audio-based turn detection (4.5% of users cut off vs 9.9% for the best alternative), and lays out the window that matters: a second and a half end to end still works, and around 600 milliseconds starts to feel human. He ends with LiveKit's open-source benchmark you can run against your own agent, a sneak peek of a voice-tuned Gemma model on LiveKit Inference, and a checklist. Ali then distinguishes a fixed LLM judge rubric from a harness that can inspect tool calls, code and external context while assessing an outcome. The budget example becomes an evaluation that checks whether returned prices actually satisfy the requested range. Agent experiments replay failure datasets against a deployed development endpoint and compare quality, latency and cost before a change ships. Setup pauses and live questions cover keys, tracing and the skills installation. The closing workflow connects automatic detection and repair to validation on real failures, with a reviewable proposal for a human to assess. The templates carry assumptions, risk, skill routing, acceptance criteria and the state of the current branch into implementation. After the agent opens a pull request, Qodo adds review findings informed by the codebase and organizational rules. The workshop shows how to inspect those findings, document fixes or deferrals and use a resolver skill to address the feedback and rerun verification. Audience questions test the boundaries: how rules are inferred and approved, how severity controls merge blocking, when verification should run again and how local checks relate to cloud review. The exercise finishes by resolving the remaining issues rather than treating a passing local run as the end of the workflow. Its reusable artifact is a structured process that keeps plans, code changes and review evidence connected. items.title: Beyond RAG: Build a Relational Context Engine from Scratch — Peter Werry, Unblocked
items.excerpt: Ask a vector store for the PRs you merged last week and it can hand back one that is semantically perfect and three years old. Peter Werry builds context engines at Unblocked, and his thesis is that RAG, meaning similarity search, is only half of retrieval. Engineering context lives in pull requests, review comments, tickets, wikis, and chat, and all of it has structure: authors, dates, states, labels, relationships. Dumping it all in a vector store and reranking fails any question with a temporal or structural half. So the other half is turning natural language into a real database query, where the model does not answer the question, it writes the query. The workshop walks six stacked pull requests that turn a stubbed query playground into a working engine over a GitHub repository. Four pieces make the query reliable. Schema discovery samples three hundred documents and merges them into one tree, with procedural code rather than a model inferring types and enums. Identity resolution maps Peter to his GitHub login with simple fuzzy matching. Query planning passes the schema, forces a name extraction tool call, and includes the current date. Validation is deny by default: an allow list of operators keeps a function clause from running JavaScript on the server, and hidden metadata fields are wiped and reinjected for tenant isolation. A retry loop feeds validation and execution errors back to the model, which exposes the need for full text search when exact match fails. The same engine then powers a chat agent, and the Q&A covers scaling schemas with summaries, continuous ingestion, why Slack holds the why questions, MCP, and hybrid search. items.text: If you want to know where all the tokens will get consumed in the future, here it is. Agent swarms will have massive implications in a number of enterprise domains like software development, cyber, life sciences research, AI research, finance, and more. The ability to parallelize agents against a unified goal where the volume of work is large, or where the search space not entirely known upfront, is going to be massive. Agents can fan out and coordinate work together on a specific mission in completely different ways from what humans are able to do. Today even in the most resource-abundant organizations, your ability to parallelize work on most projects is quite limited. Humans run into constraints on being able to communicate with one another, share status, deal with conflicts in work, keep shared context, and so on. As AI models can handle larger context without getting confused, and as they’re able to communicate effectively across their work with shared infrastructure, they can avoid many of the pitfalls that people have. You can see how this can lead to not just faster execution of tasks, but qualitatively different outcomes in medicine, research or defending against cyber attacks, scientific and math discoveries, and so on. This is why we’re going to need 1,000X more compute.

items.author: Simon Willison
items.subtitle: Simon Willison
items.title: Dwarf Fortress uses version control now
items.excerpt: I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more . That's art. I went looking and I'm sad to report that the days without version control appear to have ended. Quoting Tarn Adams over time: March 2013: "I don't use version control -- I didn't like the feeling of having the code get committed into a black box thingy with no immediate upside" March 2016: "I don’t even use version control. If you don’t know what that is then you’re not gonna yell at me. If you even know what version control is you’re gonna be like, ‘You don’t use version control? You don’t use source control? What is wrong with you? How can you even work? I’m just not cut out for it, in a sense. It’s been 15 years, so the reasons have change over time, but that’s my current understanding of it." March 2023: "I've got Discord channels to check and version control stuff to use now, so the process is definitely a little more involved" That March 2023 quote comes from an interview about the release on Steam which made them millionaires . I'm a tiny bit sad that they gave in before they hit that milestone, but what an impressive run. Tags: version-control

items.text: Agent capabilities will soon evolve at RSI pace. Agentic security (identity, permissions, observability) will need to outpace this. The evolutionary direction of the broader agents space is capability -> trust -> autonomy The first phase has been about capability - can the combination of model + harness + tools + context reliably get work done? A lot of serious work has already gone into these problems over the last couple of years. Now the challenge gets more important. and harder.

items.text: Some interesting machine & agent Vercel traffic stats. • Across the entire Vercel network, 58.18% traffic is bot-originated (last 30d). This was 32% in Jan 2024. • 60%+ of deployments on Vercel are now agentic, up from ~3% in Jan 2026. • Up to 83% of pageviews are now coming from agents to Vercel's own documentation sites. The % reliably increases the more we optimize content for them. I expect 'direct' human internet traffic to basically become a rounding error in coming years. The web will thrive, but it will be built for and by agents.

items.title: How MiniMax M3 Was Built: Sparse Attention and Native Multimodality — Olive Song
items.excerpt: Most models learn text first and get vision bolted on later. MiniMax M3 learned both from the very first training step. Olive, who works on reinforcement learning research at MiniMax, goes inside MiniMax M3, an open-weight model with frontier-level coding and agentic ability, a 1 million token context window and native multimodality. She explains MSA, MiniMax's sparse attention design (about 9x faster prefill and 15x faster decoding than full attention): an index branch that picks which blocks matter and a sparse branch that attends only to those, and why existing designs like DeepSeek's DSA didn't fit grouped-query attention or GPU memory access. Then she covers training with text and vision from step zero, why adding vision later gave unstable results, what the attention maps show, and why 3D attention inside the vision transformer improves visual understanding. In this talk: • What makes MiniMax M3 different: agentic coding, 1M context, native multimodal • How MSA sparse attention works, and why DSA didn't fit • Block-level retrieval and kernels built for real GPUs • Why training on text and vision from step zero beats adding vision later SPEAKER Olive Song, RL Lead, MiniMax X: https://x.com/olive_jy_song LINKS MiniMax: https://www.minimax.io MiniMax M3 (GitHub): https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-M3 MiniMax M3 (Hugging Face): https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3 MiniMax M3 tech report: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13392 MSA (GitHub): https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MSA CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 1:03 Meet MiniMax M3 1:37 1M token context 2:57 Sparse attention: index and sparse branches 4:17 Why not DeepSeek's DSA? 5:07 Problems with existing sparse attention 5:37 GPU memory access 7:01 MSA: what we changed 7:46 Block-level retrieval 8:21 Efficient kernels 9:01 Multi…

items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Agents spawning other agents, agents operating in the background on every task, and agent swarms will consume 1,000X more tokens than people prompting agents 1 at a time. The usage of AI as a chat system that can only work for you at the pace that you can prompt it will seem like a relic within a year or two. The vast, vast majority of tokens will be consumed by agents that are just doing continuous work for us in the background and in our workflows. This is why we’re still so early in the curve of AI agent adoption right now, and how much more compute and infrastructure build out will be needed to sustain this.

items.title: Beyond RAG: A Relational Context Engine That Cuts Token Burn — Unblocked
items.excerpt: Vector search can't answer "which PRs did I merge last week?" A relational context engine can, and it cuts token burn along the way. Peter Werry, founding engineer at Unblocked, explains what a context engine is and why coding agents need more than code search: the PRs, Slack threads and incident history that explain why the code is the way it is. He shows Claude sessions with and without that context, including one with about a 50% drop in cost and one that traced a regression to a model switch. Then he builds Unblocked's open-source document query engine step by step: automatic schema discovery, identity resolution across systems, query validation that blocks dangerous operators, retries that feed errors back to the model, and full-text search. He closes with the open-source context engine simulator for testing whether pre-gathered context helps your agents. items.excerpt: Cold starts, proprietary SDKs and one-region deployments slow AI apps down. WebAssembly at the edge removes all three. Thorsten Hans, senior developer advocate at Akamai, shows how to build and ship MCP servers and AI agents with Spin, the open-source WebAssembly framework, and run them on Akamai Functions, a globally distributed serverless platform with no cold starts. He explains why WebAssembly on the server is fast, portable and sandboxed by default, then live-codes MCP servers with wasmcp: scaffolding tools in TypeScript and Rust, composing them into a full server, testing with MCP Inspector, deploying it worldwide in about 60 seconds with one command, and calling its tools from the Zed editor. He finishes with an agent built on the Vercel AI SDK, backed by a model on a Linode GPU, and explains how memory snapshots keep apps warm. items.title: The Lethal Trifecta Is Already on Your Laptops — Michael Patterson, Coder
items.excerpt: Your coding agent can read private data, take in untrusted content and talk to the internet. That's the lethal trifecta, and it's already running on your developers' laptops. Michael Patterson, staff solutions engineer at Coder, explains Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally) and why agents like Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw running on a laptop hit all three. He covers prompt injection, what blocks big companies from rolling out agents (CISO concerns, shadow AI on personal subscriptions, alert fatigue, skeptical senior engineers), and three architectural guardrails: cloud development environments that isolate the agent, a model proxy that logs traffic and strips sensitive data before it reaches the LLM provider, and an agent firewall that denies commands and domains you didn't allow. items.title: Generation Is Cheap, Review Is Expensive: How to Stop Shipping AI Slop — Gabriel Martinez, G2i
items.excerpt: Slop isn't AI-written code. It's work that looks finished before the thinking is. Gabriel "Gabo" Martinez, engineering manager and self-described slop warden at G2i, explains what slop really is: what happens when generation outruns judgment, when ambiguity gets cleared with guesses and nobody notices there was a choice to make. He's not anti-AI, but argues we need to sober up. Code is still a liability, agents make a messy codebase messier faster, and quick prototypes convince stakeholders the hard part is done. He covers the pressure to merge faster than you can review, thousand-line PRs, 20-page AI docs that push the thinking onto reviewers, and why generation is cheap but evaluation is expensive. His fixes are conventions, diagrams as the review surface, small reviewable changes and clear ownership, inspired by Rails, plus why G2i built ORC. In this talk: • What slop is, and why it's about missing judgment, not AI • Why code is a liability and AI makes the ball of mud bigger • Incentives that push teams to merge faster than they can review • Conventions, diagrams and small changes that keep humans in control SPEAKER Gabriel Martinez, Engineering Manager, G2i LINKS ORC by G2i: https://orc.ai G2i: https://www.g2i.ai G2i on X: https://x.com/g2i_ai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:37 What slop is 1:12 The real danger: choices nobody saw 1:52 Time to sober up 2:27 What agents can't replace 2:51 How we got here 3:06 Code is a liability 4:01 A bigger ball of mud 4:11 Lines spent, not produced 5:01 Accountability 5:31 The prototype illusion 6:50 "It's not free" 7:25 Pressure to merge faster 7:45 Performance anxiety 8:45 Thousand-line PRs 9:30 The 20-page doc problem 10:14 Generation is cheap, review isn't 10:29 Twitter hype and the Ralph loop 11:39 Why code shape still matters 12:34…

items.title: Small Models, Big Results: Training a Finance Agent for Under $500 — Charles Dickens, Snorkel AI
items.excerpt: A 4 billion parameter model, trained with RL for under $500, beat its 235 billion parameter sibling on real financial questions. Charles Dickens, research scientist at Snorkel AI, shares how Snorkel and UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab trained a small model to beat a much bigger one. Working from SEC 10-K filings, they built FinQA, a financial question-answering dataset with expert-validated answers, and found even frontier models hallucinating table schemas, flooding their own context, and repeating failed strategies. Using the open-source rLLM framework and reinforcement learning with a simple pass/fail reward, they trained a Qwen3 4B model for under $500 that reached about 60% versus 51% for the 235B model. The skills transferred to harder multi-table questions without hurting general tool use. Surprisingly, simpler training data and simpler rewards worked best, because the real bottleneck was disciplined tool use, not reasoning depth. In this talk: • How the FinQA dataset was built and verified from 10-K filings • Failure modes: hallucinated schemas, context flooding, poor recovery • Training a 4B model with RL in rLLM for under $500 • Why simple data and binary rewards beat fancier setups SPEAKER Charles Dickens, Senior Applied Research Scientist, Snorkel AI LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/charles-dickens/ GitHub: https://github.com/dickensc LINKS Snorkel blog: how a 4B model outsmarted a 235B giant: https://snorkel.ai/blog/how-tool-discipline-let-a-4b-model-outsmart-a-235b-giant-on-financial-tasks/ rLLM-FinQA-4B on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/rLLM/rLLM-FinQA-4B rLLM framework: https://github.com/rllm-org/rllm Snorkel Open Benchmarks Grants: https://benchmarks.snorkel.ai/ Snorkel AI: https://snorkel.ai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:32 Specialization can beat…

items.title: Stop Prompting — Greg Pstrucha, Sentry
items.excerpt: You correct your agent. It says "You're absolutely right." Five minutes later, after compaction, it makes the same mistake again. Greg Pstrucha, who works on the infrastructure behind Seer, Sentry's debugging agent, argues you should stop re-prompting your coding agent and start codifying the rules you keep repeating. Agents have no memory, so the same elementary mistakes come back: overly defensive code, useless tests, endpoints nobody needs. Tests, strict types and especially linters turn those corrections into deterministic checks, and with agents, writing a custom lint rule is now cheap. He shows real examples from Sentry: lint rules that keep endpoints in sync with the OpenAPI schema, and a long game of whack-a-mole to keep agent skills accurate. For qualitative judgment, he uses written policies and a "Grumpy Engineer" review loop, and warns that agents will game any number you hand them, like test coverage. In this talk: • Why re-prompting fails, and why lint rules are now cheap to write • Mining your transcripts and PR reviews for rules worth enforcing • Examples from Sentry: API schema checks and linting agent skills • Policies and review agents for what linters can't catch, and why metrics get gamed SPEAKER Greg Pstrucha, Staff Software Engineer, Sentry LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/greg-pstrucha/ LINKS Sentry Seer: https://sentry.io/product/seer/ Sentry: https://sentry.io Sentry on X: https://x.com/sentry CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:38 Who still reads AI code? 1:13 The code is bad 1:58 "You're absolutely right" 2:23 Stop prompting, start codifying 2:58 Tests, strict types, linters 4:08 Why lint rules are cheap now 5:28 Mine your transcripts for rules 5:58 Custom lint rules 6:43 Example: keeping APIs in sync 7:52 Example: linting agent skills 9:17 Whack-a-m…

items.title: Building on the Codex Harness — Dominik Kundel, OpenAI
items.excerpt: Building your own agent harness is daunting. So use the one that already powers Codex. Dominik Kundel from OpenAI's Codex developer experience team explains the Codex App Server, the open-source JSON-RPC protocol that wraps the Codex harness and powers the Codex app, the IDE extensions, and third-party clients in Xcode, JetBrains and more. Using an inspector he built, he shows the real events flowing between the Codex app and the server, then covers what you can control: more than 120 client messages, sign in with ChatGPT so users bring their own subscription, developer instructions layered on top of the system prompt, dynamic and deferred tools, and per-thread model and sandbox settings. He explains how to ship the binary, generate bindings, and use the Python SDK, when to use codex exec instead, and demos Codex running inside Doom. In this talk: • What the Codex App Server is, and how it compares to ACP • Customizing the agent with developer instructions and deferred dynamic tools • Shipping the binary, generating bindings, and the Python SDK • Demo: Codex running inside Doom, with tools that change the game SPEAKER Dominik Kundel, Developer Experience, OpenAI X: https://x.com/dkundel LinkedIn: https://linkedin.com/in/dkundel LINKS Codex App Server docs: https://developers.openai.com/codex/app-server Codex on GitHub: https://github.com/openai/codex Codex SDK: https://developers.openai.com/codex/sdk CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:52 What is the App Server? 1:12 The protocol behind Codex 1:37 Open source, any model provider 2:17 How it works 3:32 Demo: inspecting live events 5:31 120+ client messages 6:31 Sign in with ChatGPT 6:56 Developer instructions 7:41 Dynamic and deferred tools 8:46 Shipping the binary 9:46 Bindings and transports 10:31 The Python SDK 10:51 Or just ask C…

items.text: There are massive startup opportunities hiding in plain sight : every layer of the computing stack will need to be rebuilt for agents. For the last few years, most of the focus has been on making enterprise software agent-ready: APIs, connectors, MCPs. Now personal agents are forcing the same conversation for consumer products - e-commerce is an early example. This is just the tip of the iceberg. Now think about the rest of the stack: Desktop and mobile OSes where agents are first-class users Cloud infra built for agents to operate directly. identity, permissions and security designed for thousands of agents acting on our behalf. Interfaces designed for agent and human users or both working together. If you’re looking for startup ideas, go through each layer of the computing stack and ask: what has to change when the primary user is an agent?

items.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
items.excerpt: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. Codex voice mode I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. Talking to my computer I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want…

items.excerpt: Release: ttok 1.0 I released ttok 0.4 , ran uv tool upgrade ttok , piped a file into the new version... and realized that it was defaulting to the GPT-4 tokenizer when it should very clearly default to GPT-5/GPT-6 instead! I figured switching the default was a reasonable excuse to finally ship a 1.0. OpenAI haven't actually confirmed that GPT-6 uses the same tokenizer as the GPT-5 family yet - there's an angry issue about it - but I found this commit by William Liu which reports on an experiment he ran confirming that the tokenizers are likely the same: All seven GPT models (5.5, 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, 6 Astra/Sol/Luna) report 44,794 tokens and match each other on every one of the 31 fixtures. GPT-6 introduces no input-count change on this corpus. Tags: projects , ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , tokenization

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: The compute needed for the stage of AI we’re about to enter is going to be insane. Personal agents, agent swarms defending enterprises, agents that review all of our code for security issues, agents that process nearly all enterprise data in workflows, background agents working on tasks 24/7, and on and on. This will take a mix of inference volume that is going to keep growing by orders of magnitude, as well as infrastructure that agents need alongside the tokens. They need computers, networking, file systems, and so on. We’re only in the early stages of what this buildout is going to look like.

items.title: Why 80% Reliability Isn't Good Enough — Felipe Blanes, Amazon AGI Lab
items.excerpt: Your agent scores great on benchmarks. Then real customers use it and it breaks. Felipe Blanes from the Amazon AGI Lab shares what he learned working directly with customers of Nova Act, Amazon's service for building browser agents, from research preview to general availability on AWS. He calls the core problem the benchmark illusion: static evals look great until customers do things nobody expected, and then all you have left is hope. His fix is an eval flywheel built around the customer: define success the way the customer does, capture signals (including by talking to customers), diagnose gaps in the model, harness or product, and feed them into decisions. He explains the trust cliff (80% reliability feels like more work; around 92% feels trustworthy), why being open about limits builds more trust than higher benchmarks, surprising use cases from Amazon Leo, Hertz and Sola, and four principles for keeping evals fresh. In this talk: • The benchmark illusion, and why static evals leave you hoping • A four-step eval flywheel driven by real customer signals • The trust cliff: why 80% reliability isn't enough • Why being open about limits builds more trust than higher scores SPEAKER Felipe Blanes, Amazon AGI Lab LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/felipeblanes/ LINKS Amazon Nova Act: https://nova.amazon.com/act Nova Act docs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/nova-act/latest/userguide/what-is-nova-act.html CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:47 What Nova Act is 1:57 Working directly with customers 2:22 The benchmark illusion 3:21 Static evals and hope 4:26 Close the customer loop 4:41 The eval flywheel 4:56 Step 1: define success 5:11 Step 2: capture signals 5:31 Talk to your customers 5:51 Step 3: diagnose gaps 6:56 Step 4: feed decisions 7:26 Four stages of the customer journey 9:35 Les…

items.title: We Mapped 115 Microservices for Our Coding Agents — Kamalakannan Nandagopal, Postman
items.excerpt: Coding agents are great inside one repo. Postman has 115 microservices and thousands of endpoints. Kamalakannan Nandagopal, staff engineer at Postman, shares how Postman made coding agents work across a real distributed system. Docs go stale, skills and MCPs are only as good as their context, and agent memory stays stuck with one person. Borrowing from Postman's go-to-market team, they realized APIs are the context layer, and built an API context graph that maps every service, endpoint, implementation and call, all the way down to databases, with every data point grounded in code or production telemetry. He shares evals built from real PRs and design decisions: big wins on API discovery, redesign and impact assessment, an honest failure when the graph went stale, the finding that 75% of PRs touched APIs, and a 21-page architecture review the agent produced on its own. In this talk: • Why coding agents struggle with distributed systems and microservices • Building an API context graph grounded in code and telemetry • Eval results on API discovery, redesign and impact assessment • Why keeping the graph fresh matters as much as building it SPEAKER Kamalakannan Nandagopal, Staff Engineer, Postman LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/kamalakannan-nandagopal-3650818a/ LINKS Postman Context Graph API: https://blog.postman.com/introducing-the-context-graph-api-one-map-of-your-api-ecosystem/ Context Graph docs: https://learning.postman.com/docs/use/context-graph/get-started Postman: https://www.postman.com Postman on X: https://x.com/getpostman CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:32 115 microservices 1:02 From autocomplete to autonomous agents 1:42 Real systems are distributed 2:12 Docs go stale 2:36 Skills, MCPs and agent memory 3:21 What the go-to-market team learned 4:01 APIs are the con…

items.author: @danshipper
items.subtitle: Dan Shipper · ceo @every | the only subscription you need…
items.text: OpenAI’s Dots launched last week and they've taken over @every. A few things that stand out: They protect your attention. Over the weekend, my Dot posted my model-testing results to Slack and brought back replies. I could keep working without opening Slack and disappearing down a rabbit hole. My weekend stayed pretty clear and calm. They’re useful for the little things you miss. People at Every are using them to pull important information out of school emails, catch missed Slack messages, and flag account-access requests. Voice makes them useful away from your laptop. Our head of video was talking his Dot through video edits while running around getting our launch out. The ecosystem matters. Dots feel roughly at feature parity with Muse, Instinct, and Grok bots. But having an agent connected to the ecosystem you already use for work and life is a real advantage. If you use ChatGPT, I recommend trying one. Permissions are still frustrating. I have to approve the same basic thing multiple times, and sometimes even after I approve it, my Dot says it can’t do it. That needs to get fixed. I’m less convinced we’ll stay loyal to the characters. Mine is named Boo, and I’m attached to him. But I felt that way about my OpenClaw agent, too. When something better comes along, I switch. In a year, I expect to be using a persistent agent. Boo will probably be dead. RIP, Boo. I get into all of this at the start of this week’s podcast, and then sit down with @bigwilliestyle to talk about where we go from here. In a lot of ways, Dots and GrokBots remind me of a wave we went through with OpenClaw eight months ago. We talk about personal vs. company agents, why we built our own company agent, and whether companies will end up with a whole shadow org chart of agents. Full episode below.

items.title: Your AI Agent Has No Nervous System — Matt Gibiec, Dynatrace
items.excerpt: Your coding agent is fast. But it can't see how your services actually run, so it guesses. Matt Gibiec, who leads AI-native solutions engineering at Dynatrace, explains why AI agents need something like a nervous system: real context from the environment they're changing. Agents get stuck in loops, cause operational and security issues, and are hard to measure, because they work fast but blind, only as good as the data they can see. He introduces Bluebox by Dynatrace, an observability agent for your coding agent, and walks through scenarios: bringing production dependencies into local testing so a change that works on your laptop doesn't break three other services, spotting issues before users feel them, suggesting fixes that account for the rest of the system, and briefing agents with real usage data before they build, with a human keeping final control. In this talk: • Why agents loop, hallucinate and break things without environment context • Bringing production dependencies into local testing • Catching problems early and tying them to the change that caused them • Planning before you prompt, with a human approving the final fix SPEAKER Matt Gibiec, Solutions Engineering, AI Native, Dynatrace LINKS Bluebox by Dynatrace: https://bluebox.ai Dynatrace: https://www.dynatrace.com Bluebox on X: https://x.com/Blueboxhq CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:35 About Dynatrace 1:00 What the title means 2:10 Stuck in a loop 2:50 Operations and security 3:30 How do you measure value? 4:34 Fast, but blind 6:34 Context is king 7:04 Introducing Bluebox 7:29 Works locally, breaks in production 9:09 Catch issues before users do 10:59 Fix without breaking other things 12:09 Plan before you prompt 13:29 A human stays in control 14:44 Try the preview Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 in…

items.excerpt: Agents finish a task, then forget what they learned. Retrieval alone won't fix that. Will Lyon, senior product manager at Neo4j, explains why agent memory built on embeddings and retrieval isn't enough: recall isn't actionable knowledge. Agents need knowledge that is connected, typed and traceable. He shows Neo4j's model of agent memory as a context graph with short-term, long-term and reasoning memory, covering entity extraction and resolution, shared ontologies, and decision traces that let many agents learn from each other. Then he turns memory into action: distilling grounded, governed skills from the graph, based on Neo4j research that treats skills as typed execution graphs, with checks for grounding, coverage and coherence, and alerts when a skill goes stale. He demos the Neo4j Agent Memory Service distilling a patient-intake skill from a healthcare conversation. items.title: Grep or Embeddings? Agentic Search Over Company Documents — George He, LlamaIndex
items.excerpt: Grep works great on a codebase. Try it on millions of PDFs, slides and scanned schematics. George He, head of engineering at LlamaIndex, explains when agents need pre-indexed search and when plain file traversal is enough. Claude Code skipped embeddings because code is small, text-based, local and full of breadcrumbs. Company data is huge, messy, multimodal and permissioned. He shows how to give an agent a harness of tools so it can choose: hybrid retrieval as a compass, then listing, metadata filtering, grep and reading to dig in, plus parsed text and page screenshots for complex documents. He covers parsing with LlamaParse and the open-source LiteParse, permissions and freshness in production, and the ingest-parse-index pipeline. Then he demos an agent building a cash-flow table from 135 Alphabet financial filings, grounded in the source files. items.title: AI Hackers Are Faster Than Your Pen Test — Eli Cohen, Snyk
items.excerpt: Attackers use AI too, and the fastest AI attack he cites took four minutes. A pen test once or twice a year can't keep up. Eli Cohen of Snyk, co-founder of the runtime security company Helios, explains why security has to go on the offense in an agent-first world. Developers now ship far more code, much of it insecure, while attackers use frontier models to chain small vulnerabilities into critical ones in minutes. He walks through why traditional tools fall short: static scanning misses runtime issues, dynamic testing misses business logic, and human pen tests are expensive and happen only a few times a year. Then he describes continuous offensive security: AI pen testing on every code change, agent red teaming, and a team of agents (orchestrator, recon, vulnerability hunters, an exploit-validating judge, remediation and reporting), fed with context from other scanners. He ends with four questions to ask any AI pen testing vendor. items.title: From 36% to 100%: How Self-Improving Agents Write Their Own Skills — Rafal Wilinski, Runlayer
items.excerpt: When one agent finally cracks a hard problem, what if every agent in the company learned it too? Rafal Wilinski, founding engineer at Runlayer, shows how to go from one self-improving agent to a self-improving company. He explains why skills matter more as agents work longer (a bad start can send them down an hours-long rabbit hole) and the three problems holding skills back: they're built for developers, nobody has time to write them, and many clients don't support them. His fix is to deliver skills over MCP from one governed server, then let agents write their own skills by distilling successful and failed runs, an idea borrowed from the Voyager Minecraft paper. In one test, a distilled skill took a task from 36% success to 100%. Multiply that across every agent and you get an organizational flywheel that keeps your hard-won knowledge even as models change. items.excerpt: As previously promised , here's Anthropic's new fast, low cost model: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 . The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago , and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna , released last month. The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna - $0.10/$0.50 - up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75. Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there's a hidden price increase there. If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal. The most recent release of llm-anthropic finally fixed it so I don't need to ship a new version of that plugin for every new model. In particular, Result 003, the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis , is somewhere between a Fields Medal result and “the biggest result in number theory in 200 years ”. items.excerpt: I was a graph theory junkie long ago and even moved to Budapest for awhile to study among the greats. While I was there I started working on Barnette's Conjecture which came to occupy my thoughts over the next 24 years of my life, on and off as I worked in many different fields. I spent thousands of hours on that problem. I really enjoyed it. Hearing that it is solved somehow makes me sad in a far-off way, like hearing an ex-girlfriend died suddenly in a car crash. items.title: The Self-Improving OSS Agent Stack — Marc Klingen, Langfuse
items.excerpt: Improving an agent used to mean a human reading traces every week. Now agents can do most of that loop for you. Marc Klingen, co-founder of Langfuse, shows how teams are moving from manually improving their agents to letting AI run the improvement loop. He explains the reference stack that emerged for building agents, which connects online tracing and monitoring with offline datasets, experiments and evals, and maps the layers of loops from next-token prediction up to human goal-setting. AI is already good at proposing fixes, and teams are starting to use it to maintain datasets and eval criteria too, while humans stay in charge of direction. In a demo, a coding agent uses Langfuse's agent skills to find that Langfuse's own changelog writer leaks internal jargon, updates the evals, and back-tests a better version before shipping it. items.excerpt: AI changed how we write code. But 70% of engineering time goes to running and fixing it. Varun Krovvidi, product marketing lead at Resolve AI, explains why AI that writes code well still struggles to run production. Code is self-documenting, modular and a single domain. Production spans code, infrastructure, telemetry and many teams, and needs one correct answer. He covers where agents crack as you scale: anchoring bias and the model treadmill, too much or too little context, coherent answers that aren't causal, missing guardrails, and no learning across investigations. Then he lays out six pillars of a harness that fixes them: model orchestration, context engineering, causal reasoning, governed actions, learning systems and evals. He finishes with a demo of Resolve AI turning a Grafana alert into a root cause, ruling out a coincidental GCP outage, and holding its ground when pushed. items.excerpt: Release: llm-openai-decisions 0.1a0 OpenAI released their new Jev-style Decisions API , as previously announced at last week's DevDay. Since I already have an llm-typesafe plugin for talking to Jev, I had GPT-6 Astra read the new OpenAI API documentation and build an llm-openai-decisions plugin inspired by llm-typesafe . Unlike Jev, the new gpt-6-luna decision model supports image input in addition to text. Both models charge for input it and not for output: OpenAI's is 10 cents per million input tokens, Jev's is 4.2 cents per million. Otherwise the API shape is very similar to Jev, at least conceptually. Jev supports three question types for yes/no, choices, or scores. OpenAI Decisions supports the same three types. Install the plugin like this: llm install llm-openai-decisions Here's an example query against an image attachment: llm -m openai-decisions/gpt-6-luna \ -a https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2025/two-pelicans.jpg \ -s ' Does this image contain any mammals? ' And example output: { "type" : " predicate " , "name" : " evaluation " , "probability" : 0.0 } Consult the README for full details of how to run the other types of questions. Tags: openai , llm , coding-agents , jev

items.excerpt: In a software factory, agents write everything your users get. Your engineers build the factory. Dru Knox, head of product and design at Tessl, explains harness engineering (some now call it loop engineering), the discipline that takes a team from using coding agents to running a software factory. He defines a factory by three metrics: autonomy, automation and quality. He breaks the work into inner, outer and meta loops, and explains why harness engineering is hard: the field changes weekly, the work is unplanned, and the signals you need are stuck in local logs. items.text: Introducing gdp-ts: Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript. gdp-ts is a library, linter and AI skill for safer API design. Under this contract, sensitive functions require 'proofs' that the caller performed an authorization check. The typechecker verifies these proofs at compile time, preventing your team and agents from shipping catastrophic security (and other kinds of) bugs. While these patterns have existed for quite some time, especially in ecosystems like Haskell, ① human code review and ② cognitive and syntactic overhead made these solutions niche. The situation is now inverted. Agents are writing more code than we can review, and they *thrive* in tight loops with hard constraints that would frustrate us. We see this with the rise of Rust, borrow checker, code aesthetics debate and all. The README and examples model a real-world Vercel API product constraint: changing the password on a Project requires a proof of a certain role + a certain entitlement. Thanks to Matt Noonan and Ollie Charles for their research in this space. https://t.co/eRWdiMvQ2V
